guided.title: Two definitions of an active customer
guided.prompt: Count the customers that are active in 2025-06 under two definitions: (a) at least one order in the month, (b) at least three distinct orders in the month. Print `any <n>` and `three_plus <m>` on two lines.
guided.starter:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
countries = ["UK", "Germany", "France", "Spain"]
cats = ["Hardware", "Software", "Services"]
customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": range(1, 41),
    "customer_name": [f"Customer {i:02d}" for i in range(1, 41)],
    "country": [countries[i % 4] for i in range(40)],
    "segment": [["Retail", "Corporate"][(i // 4) % 2] for i in range(40)],
})
products = pd.DataFrame({
    "product_id": range(1, 13),
    "product_name": [f"Product {i:02d}" for i in range(1, 13)],
    "category": [cats[i % 3] for i in range(12)],
    "unit_cost": [float(10 + 5 * i) for i in range(12)],
})
n = 400
sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": range(1, n + 1),
    "order_date": pd.to_datetime("2025-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.integers(0, 365, n), unit="D"),
    "customer_id": rng.integers(1, 41, n),
    "product_id": rng.integers(1, 13, n),
    "quantity": rng.integers(1, 6, n),
})
sales["unit_price"] = (sales["product_id"].map(products.set_index("product_id")["unit_cost"]) * 1.5).round(2)
calendar = pd.DataFrame({"date": pd.date_range("2025-01-01", "2025-12-31")})
calendar["year"] = calendar["date"].dt.year
calendar["quarter"] = calendar["date"].dt.quarter
calendar["month_number"] = calendar["date"].dt.month
calendar["month_name"] = calendar["date"].dt.strftime("%B")
sales["revenue"] = sales["quantity"] * sales["unit_price"]
fact = (sales.merge(customers, on="customer_id").merge(products, on="product_id")
        .merge(calendar, left_on="order_date", right_on="date"))

# June orders per customer

guided.title: Define and tree a metric (written)
guided.prompt: For a subscription business, define 'monthly recurring revenue' (MRR) with numerator, denominator (if any), window, grain and filters, and draw its metric tree to at least three leaves. Say which leaf you would treat as leading and why.
guided.solution: Definition: MRR is the sum, over active paying subscriptions at the end of the calendar month, of the monthly price (annual plans divided by 12), after discounts, excluding one-off fees and free trials; grain is the subscription, window the calendar month, no denominator. Tree: MRR = active subscriptions x average revenue per subscription. Active subscriptions = subscriptions at the start of the month + new - churned. Average revenue per subscription = list price x (1 - average discount) x plan mix. Leading leaf: trial sign-ups or qualified trials this month, because they precede new paying subscriptions by days or weeks; this must be tested by correlating this month's trials with next month's new subscriptions. MRR itself is lagging.
rubric: Definition includes numerator, window, grain and filters.
Tree has at least three leaves that rebuild MRR.
Names a plausible leading indicator and says it must be tested.
hints: What counts as recurring and what does not?
Subscriptions times price per subscription is a start.
Which driver moves before revenue does?

independent.title: Design a metric tree for a problem (written, stretch)
independent.prompt: A retailer's online conversion has fallen. Design a metric tree for online revenue with at least three levels, mark which metrics are leading and which lagging, name two vanity metrics to avoid in the report, and say which leaves you would examine first to explain the fall and why.
independent.starter:
Tree: ...
Leading / lagging: ...
Vanity to avoid: ...
Examine first: ...
independent.solution: Tree: online revenue = sessions x conversion rate x average order value. Sessions = new visitors + returning visitors. Conversion rate = product page to basket rate x basket to checkout rate x checkout completion rate. Average order value = items per order x price per item. Leading: sessions, product page views, basket additions (they precede orders); lagging: orders, revenue, returns. Vanity: total page views and cumulative registered users, which rise regardless of performance. Examine first: the three conversion steps separately, because a fall in conversion shows in one of them (for example a checkout completion problem after a release), then the split of sessions by source to see whether a change of traffic mix lowered conversion. Check the funnel by device and by week to separate a real change from a tracking issue.
rubric: Tree has three levels and multiplies or adds to revenue.
Names vanity metrics that cannot fall or guide action.
Chooses leaves to examine first with reasons.

checks.question: Which is NOT part of a complete metric definition?
checks.explanation: A definition needs the numerator, the denominator if a ratio, the window, the grain and the filters. Colour belongs to presentation.

checks.question: Orders = customers x orders per customer. Customers 40 and orders per customer 10 in both years, units per order from 1.8 to 3.0. Which driver explains revenue growth?
checks.explanation: Customers and orders per customer are unchanged, so the revenue change comes from the basket: units per order (with price per unit a tiny part).

checks.question: An indicator has correlation 0.62 with this month's revenue and -0.24 with next month's. What do you conclude?
options: It is a strong leading indicator
It moves with the same month; it is not shown to lead
checks.explanation: A leading indicator should relate to the later outcome. Here the relationship is concurrent, and with twelve points even that is weak evidence.

checks.question: Which metric is most clearly a vanity metric?
checks.explanation: A cumulative count can only rise, so it flatters whatever happens and rarely guides a decision. The others can fall and tie to actions.

checks.question: In sequential substitution, why state the order of the drivers?
options: The split between drivers depends on the order when several change together
checks.explanation: The total change is the same, but the joint effect of drivers changing together is assigned to whichever is substituted later, so the order affects the split.
